content: 1. The allocation sequence in studies conducted in Liberia was not clearly described, and in the case of Côte d’Ivoire, it was either unclear or not concealed. Other criteria for assessing the risk of bias (ROB) were also unclear. However, the source of funding was deemed to have a low risk of bias. 2. Circulating filarial antigen (CFA) is considered an indirect marker of treatment efficacy. The absence or clearance of CFA indicates the absence of infection with adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms. Conversely, the presence of CFA suggests infection with male worms, fertile or non-fertile female worms, or even dead adult worms of W. bancrofti. 3. A randomized controlled trial by Tafataha et al. (2015) evaluated the impact of increased doses and frequencies of albendazole and ivermectin on the clearance of W. bancrofti microfilariae in northern Malawi. Another study (NCT01905436, 2017) focused on optimizing mass drug administration (MDA) regimens for lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis in Côte d’Ivoire. 4. A single-arm community cohort study by Pion et al. (2017) assessed the effect of biannual albendazole administration on microfilarial prevalence. After 15 months, only 1 out of 12 patients (<10%) achieved microfilarial clearance with 600 mg of albendazole. Similarly, an 8% reduction in CFA prevalence was observed, but no patients achieved antigen clearance after 15 months of treatment. 5. The study by Ismail et al. (1998) was indirectly compared to the findings of Pion et al. (2017). The small sample size (N=12) in the latter study limited the robustness of the comparison. 6. The wide confidence intervals in the Swiss TPH/SCIH study (Lymphatic Filariasis A-21) highlight the variability in treatment outcomes. CFA remains an indirect measure of treatment efficacy, and its presence or absence provides insights into the infection status with W. bancrofti adult worms. 7. The CASP quality assessment tool was adapted to evaluate qualitative studies included in the scoping review. Several studies demonstrated moderate to severe concerns due to poor reporting of qualitative methodologies and findings. For example, Amarillo (2008) and Babu (2004, 2010) studies had issues with unclear sampling and inadequate separation of quantitative and qualitative data. 8. Studies such as Baker (2007) and da-Costa Vroom (2015) highlighted challenges in integrating lymphatic filariasis elimination programs into primary healthcare systems and data reporting constraints in MDA activities, respectively. 9. Community perceptions and barriers to MDA compliance were explored in studies like King (2011) and Kisoka (2016). These studies emphasized the importance of addressing community-directed dilemmas and improving participation to enhance program effectiveness. 10. The systematic review by Krentel (2012) introduced causal chain mapping as a novel method to analyze treatment compliance decisions in lymphatic filariasis elimination programs. 11. The qualitative scoping review included studies from diverse settings, such as Amarillo et al. (2008) in the Philippines, Babu et al. (2004, 2010) in India, and Baker et al. (2007) in the Dominican Republic. These studies provided insights into factors influencing MDA acceptance, compliance, and operational challenges. 12. The WHO guidelines for alternative MDA regimens for lymphatic filariasis elimination were developed based on systematic reviews and modeling studies. These guidelines emphasized the importance of evidence-based approaches to optimize treatment strategies. 13. The GRADE handbook (2013) and Cochrane Handbook (2011) were referenced for grading the quality of evidence and synthesizing qualitative research, respectively. These tools provided a framework for evaluating the strength of recommendations and methodological rigor. 14. Studies like Glenton et al. (2013) and Munro et al. (2007) synthesized qualitative evidence on barriers and facilitators to implementing health worker programs and patient adherence to treatment, respectively. These findings informed strategies to improve access to healthcare in low-resource settings. 15. The systematic review by Coffeng et al. (2014) modeled the impact of increasing ivermectin treatment frequency for onchocerciasis elimination. Similarly, studies on lymphatic filariasis highlighted the efficacy and safety of co-administered diethylcarbamazine, albendazole, and ivermectin. 16. The findings from these studies underscore the need for robust methodologies, clear reporting, and community engagement to optimize MDA programs for lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis elimination.
